title: Batcher coalescence dead-window causing tail latency spikes and tenant unfairness
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Summary: During a capacity ramp on 2026-02-08 we observed intermittently elevated 99.9th-percentile tail latency for the continuous batcher subsystem across several customer tenants. In parallel, lower-priority tenant requests experienced extended queuing while higher-priority tenants saw normal service — indicating a fairness regression. This ticket captures the incident analysis, temporary mitigations, and planned action items to prevent recurrence.
impact: Multiple hosted customers experienced request latency spikes (95th->99.9th increases of 3x) for 18 minutes during the event window. Two customers filed performance alerts; no data loss or correctness regressions were reported. The event correlated with a sudden shift in traffic mix (many short sequences with bursty arrivals) causing unexpected batch coalescence behavior.
timeline:
- 2026-02-08 10:12 UTC: Autoscaler added capacity upstream; traffic mix shifted (short requests surge)
- 10:14 UTC: Continuous batcher metrics show a growing population of partially filled coalesced batches with stale wait timestamps (dead-window)
- 10:16 UTC: Tail latency alerts fire (runtime-ops and on-call Page)
- 10:18 UTC: On-call rotates to batching owner; temporary policy to reduce coalescence window rolled out to all hosts (10:25 UTC)
- 10:30 UTC: Tail latency begins recovering as batches flush more aggressively
- 10:35 UTC: Full recovery observed; post-incident telemetry retained and tracing enabled for deeper analysis
reproduction_steps:
1) Simulate traffic with mixed short/long sequences and bursty arrivals (Poisson bursts of short sequences interleaved with steady long requests).
2) Configure continuous-batcher with default coalescence window and no per-tenant preemptive-flush.
3) Observe batches accumulating with high variance in wait times and KV cache pressure causing backpressure.
4) Monitor 99.9th tail latency; it should spike under these conditions.
root_cause: The continuous batcher uses a time-based coalescence window optimized for steady-state workloads. During a sudden traffic-mix change the coalescence logic accumulated many partially filled batches that waited until the window expiry instead of being flushed early. A concurrent change to priority sharding reduced the effectiveness of the per-tenant fairness limiter, allowing some shards to dominate GPU batch slots. Combined, these led to increased tail latency and unfair queueing.
short_term_mitigation:
- Rolled out a global reduction of the coalescence window from 20ms -> 5ms as an emergency measure.
- Enabled preemptive-flush heuristic (experimental) for batches older than 8ms.
- Reverted the recent priority-sharding tweak on the fleet to restore the fairness limiter behavior.
- Added alerting on 'average batch fill time' to detect recurrence earlier.
long_term_mitigation:
- Implement adaptive coalescence: adjust per-host coalescence window based on observed arrival entropy and sequence-length histogram.
- Introduce a per-tenant token budget for active batch slots to bound resource capture by noisy tenants.
- Add a 'stale-batch circuit breaker' that preempts and flushes batches exceeding a configurable age threshold when overall worker saturation is high.
- Revise priority-sharding implementation to respect fairness limiter invariants; add unit/integration tests to prevent regressions.
- Expand integration tests to include mixed traffic fuzz harness (short/long bursts) and assert tail-latency SLOs.

metrics_and_observability_changes:
- Added 'batch_fill_time_ms' histogram at host and shard level.
- Introduced 'stale_batch_count' gauge and 'preemptive_flush_count' counter.
- New dashboard tile: batcher fairness heatmap by tenant.
- Tracing: emitted batch lifecycle span including enqueue_time, flush_reason, and tenant_token_balance.
postmortem_notes:
- The emergency reduction of the coalescence window mitigated impact but increased GPU kernel invocation rate; we must balance cost vs latency.
- Fairness regressions are subtle and can be triggered by innocuous sharding changes; we need stronger invariants in code and tests.
- Communication: two affected customers were proactively contacted by CSMs; a short incident summary was posted to the status page and customers Slack channel.
- Consider scheduled chaos tests for batcher to catch policy conflicts under capacity changes.
